courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
question: Why does the sort key put the tile ID in the high bits and the depth in the low bits, rather than the reverse?
options: So a single sort groups instances by tile first, and orders each tile's instances by depth
Because depth needs more than 32 bits of precision
So that far Gaussians are drawn first, as in the painter's algorithm
Because radix sort only looks at the low 32 bits
explain: Sorting by a combined key orders by its high bits first. With tile ID on top, all instances of a tile become contiguous, and ties within a tile are broken by depth, giving a front-to-back list per tile from one global sort.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Finding room for the tag: wide CAS, spare bits, indices
question: Your nodes come from a pool of at most 4 billion entries. Which layout lets you avoid both double-width CAS and spare pointer bits?
options: 32-bit array index and 32-bit tag in one 64-bit word
64-bit pointer and 64-bit tag
48-bit pointer and 16-bit tag
explain: This is the array-index option from Michael and Scott: an index into a node array needs only 32 bits for up to 2^32 nodes, leaving 32 bits for the counter, and an ordinary 64-bit CAS covers both.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
question: A colleague's ablation script sorts each run's per-query scores from best to worst before running a paired t-test. The test reports p < 0.001 for a stage. What went wrong?
options: Sorting broke the pairing: deltas now compare different queries, so the p-value is meaningless
Nothing; a paired t-test is invariant to the order of the queries
The t-test should have been replaced by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The p-value is fine but should be divided by the number of queries
explain: Pairing works only if position i holds the same query in both runs. Sorting each run separately pairs the best query of one run with the best of the other, removing query-level noise artificially. Align runs by query id before differencing.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
question: Which change actually fixes the vulnerable handler?
options: Switching the route from GET to POST so the id is in the body
Adding owner_id = the session user's id to the query, and returning 404 when no row matches
Encrypting the id in the URL
Adding a CAPTCHA before showing invoices
explain: Moving the id into the body or encrypting it changes where the id travels, not whether the server checks it. Only an ownership condition based on the server-side session makes a foreign id return nothing.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Client-side-only checks, tampering, and trusting what the client sends
question: A Next.js app's only login check is in middleware. Which lesson from CVE-2025-29927 applies to every framework?
options: Middleware should be removed entirely
Do not let one layer be the sole authorization check; verify access again where the data is read
Use a longer session cookie
Block all requests with a Referer header
explain: The bug let clients skip the middleware layer. Apps that also checked authorization in their route handlers or data access were not exposed by that skip. Vercel itself advises not to rely on middleware alone.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Access control models: ACL, RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC (Google Zanzibar)
question: A hospital wants: doctors may read a patient record only while they are assigned to that patient and only from hospital networks. Which model expresses that directly?
options: ABAC: it combines attributes of the subject, the object and the environment
RBAC: a doctor role
An ACL on each hospital network
Capabilities given to patients
explain: A doctor role says nothing about which patient or which network. ABAC policies combine the user's assignment, the record's patient and the request's network, the kind of rule NIST SP 800-162 describes.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Privileged groups, and why so many paths lead to Domain Admins
question: An attacker adds a permission to the AdminSDHolder object granting their account full control. What happens within about an hour?
options: Nothing, AdminSDHolder is only a template for new domains
The DC deletes the attacker's account
Windows Defender blocks the change
SDProp copies the AdminSDHolder permissions onto protected accounts and groups, so the attacker gains control of them
explain: SDProp resets protected objects to the AdminSDHolder template every 60 minutes by default. A planted entry is copied to every admin account and group, which makes AdminSDHolder a persistence target to monitor.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
question: Contoso enforces AES for all service tickets. The svc_backup account (SPN set, password 'Backup2016') still worries you. Why?
options: AES tickets cannot be requested by normal users
AES tickets are encrypted with krbtgt instead
It does not: AES fully prevents Kerberoasting
AES makes each guess slower, but a short dictionary-style password is still cracked quickly from wordlists
explain: AES with PBKDF2 raises the cost per guess, but wordlists try 'Backup2016' style passwords early. The password itself must be long and random, ideally managed by Windows as a gMSA.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
question: A 4662 shows AccessMask 0x100 with GUID 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 and subject `DC02$`. Should you page the incident team?
options: Yes, any 4662 with that GUID is DCSync
Yes, because DC computer accounts never replicate
No, 4662 cannot record replication
Probably not: `DC02$` is a domain controller account and replication between DCs is normal; alert on non-DC subjects
explain: Replicating Directory Changes All is exercised by DCs all day. The signal is the same request from an account that is not a DC.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
question: Which of these is NOT a protection Protected Users applies at the DC?
options: Members cannot authenticate with NTLM
Members cannot use DES or RC4 in Kerberos pre-authentication
Members' TGTs cannot be renewed beyond four hours
Members' passwords are rotated every 30 days automatically
explain: Automatic password rotation is what gMSAs and LAPS do. Protected Users blocks NTLM, weak Kerberos types, delegation and long-lived TGTs.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: VBA macros: where the code hides and how olevba reads it
question: A document's macro source looks harmless, yet in a sandbox with a matching Office version it starts PowerShell. Which explanation fits ATT&CK's description?
options: The PROJECT stream is encrypted
VBA stomping: the compiled p-code differs from the source, and Office ran the p-code
The mini stream is corrupt
The document has no macros and PowerShell started on its own
explain: T1564.007: when the Office version matches the one recorded in _VBA_PROJECT, the stored p-code runs, so the source shown by source-only tools can be a decoy. Disassemble the p-code with pcodedmp and compare.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, disk images and containers: the post-macro lures
question: Two lure shortcuts from campaigns a month apart have the same TrackerDataBlock MachineID. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: They were probably built on the same machine: a lead for clustering the campaigns, to confirm with other evidence
They target the same victim machine
It is the NetBIOS name of the email server
MachineID is random per file, so it is a coincidence
explain: The MachineID is the NetBIOS name where the link target last resided, typically the builder's machine. Shared values are a strong clustering lead, not proof: they can be copied or faked.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking I: what a packed file looks like, using UPX
question: Why does a packed program import LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress but almost nothing else?
options: Packers delete imports to save space only
Those are the only functions Windows allows
The stub resolves the real imports by name at run time, after unpacking
The program does not use any Windows functions
explain: With those two functions the stub can load any DLL and look up any function by name, so the original import table can stay compressed until run time.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
question: In the toy, with 6 known files there are 12 groups but the victim file is still unreadable. Why?
options: The victim file uses the wrong cipher
At least one byte pair the victim's keystream needs still spans two groups
Union-find needs exactly 8 files
The master key changed after file 6
explain: Decryption needs the XOR of each pair the victim's file uses. If any pair spans two groups, that relation is unknown. File 7's equations merged the last needed groups.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Information leaks: why modern exploits start by reading
question: Why does strong address randomization make information leaks more valuable to attackers, not less?
options: Because with addresses hidden, a leak is often the only reliable way to learn where targets are, so it becomes a required step
Because randomization creates new bugs
Because leaks disable randomization permanently
Because randomization only applies to leaked memory
explain: Randomization forces the attacker to learn addresses. A leak is the cheapest way to do that, so it becomes a standard rung of the ladder. The kernel self-protection guide makes this exact point about KASLR.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: From use-after-free to type confusion, and how it is closed
question: Which defence most directly prevents the demo's confusion while leaving the bug in place?
options: Type isolation, so a session slot can never be refilled by a note
A stack canary
A larger ASLR entropy
Disabling the JIT
explain: Type isolation removes the cross-type reuse that the confusion depends on. Canaries and ASLR are unrelated to heap object lifetime. The bug should still be fixed, ideally caught first by ASan or CodeQL.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Kernel cases: EternalBlue's size bug and Dirty Pipe's stale flag
question: According to Microsoft's analysis, what was true of EternalBlue on fully updated 64-bit Windows 10 with virtualization-based security, before MS17-010 was applied?
options: The bug was present, but the leaked exploit's assumptions failed: the target region was not executable and was randomized, the hypervisor enforced kernel W^X, and kCFG checked the final indirect call
The bug was absent
The exploit worked unchanged
SMB was disabled by default
explain: Mitigations changed the cost of exploitation, not the bug. Patching remained the only fix.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
question: A team can afford only one of these this quarter for a C media parser reachable from incoming messages. Which gives the biggest reduction in exploitable risk?
options: Running it under coverage-guided fuzzing with AddressSanitizer and fixing what is found, then moving it into a tight sandbox
Raising ASLR entropy on the parser process
Adding a stack canary to main()
Renaming the process
explain: Fuzzing with sanitizers removes real bugs before attackers find them, and sandboxing limits what any remaining bug can reach. ASLR and canaries are worth having but each guards a single rung.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Rules of engagement for a red team
question: Why does the pre-action check test the halt flag before anything else?
options: It is faster
The halt flag is optional
Python requires it
A halt must stop every action regardless of window, target or activity type
explain: Order matters: if the halt were checked last, a bug or missing field earlier in the function could let an action through after the control group said stop.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Atomic Red Team: testing one technique at a time
question: Why do atomic tests carry a stable GUID in addition to a name and number?
options: To encrypt the test
Because YAML requires it
So the SOC cannot see the test
So results can be matched to the exact same test across library updates, when numbering may change
explain: Test numbers within a technique can shift as tests are added or removed. A GUID pins your results and regression history to one specific test.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: CISA's red team at a critical infrastructure organisation
question: Which single finding enabled the team to impersonate any account for the rest of the assessment?
options: Users clicked a phishing link
Music software was installed on servers
Passwords were changed every 60 days
The krbtgt key, unchanged for over a decade, was taken through DCSync and used to forge tickets
explain: With the krbtgt key, the team forged golden tickets for any account. Rotating krbtgt twice (with the wait) invalidates forged tickets; *Active Directory attacks* covers why both resets are needed.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
question: A retest of a fixed finding still fails. What should happen next?
options: Mark it fixed anyway, since work was done
Remove the test from the suite
Return to the root cause: the diagnosis or the fix was wrong
Blame the red team
explain: A failed retest means the gap is not where the team thought, for example a rule was written but the log source is not reaching the SIEM. Re-diagnosing is the point of retesting.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
question: An agent makes the correct database change in tau-retail but never asks the user to confirm, which the policy requires. What reward does the paper's grader give?
options: 1, because the final database matches and the required outputs appear
0, because policy violations are detected from the transcript
0.5 as partial credit
It depends on the user simulator's satisfaction rating
explain: The reward checks only the final database and required output strings. The paper notes r = 1 is necessary but not sufficient for a good episode, and gives this exact case: a return issued without explicit confirmation.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
question: After compaction the agent starts ignoring a formatting rule the user gave in their very first message. What is the most robust fix?
options: Disable compaction
Repeat the rule in every tool description
Put the rule in a persistent instruction file or system prompt that is sent on every request
Lower max_turns so compaction never triggers
explain: A summary may paraphrase or omit early instructions. Anything that must hold for the whole session belongs in content the harness re-sends on every call, which compaction never rewrites.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Main context vs external context: paging memory like an OS
question: You give an agent a 2,000-character in-context profile block and an unlimited archival store. Where should "user's company VPN requires the --legacy flag" go if it matters in about one task per month?
options: The in-context block, because in-context facts are always used correctly
Archival storage, because it is rarely needed and would waste always-on block space
Neither; facts that rarely matter should be dropped
Both, so the agent can cross-check them
explain: The in-context block is paid for on every turn and capped in size, so it should hold small facts that are relevant almost every turn. A monthly detail belongs in external storage, retrieved when a VPN task comes up. Storing it twice creates two copies that can drift apart when one is updated.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
question: Which defense addresses the persistence attack most directly?
options: Store a source tag on every memory and never treat tool- or web-derived memories as user instructions
Use a larger context window so the memory store is not needed
Lower the recency decay so old memories fade faster
Run reflection more often so injected memories get summarized away
explain: The attack works because text from an untrusted web page is written and later read back as trusted user knowledge. Provenance breaks that chain. Faster decay only delays it (and retrieval refreshes recency), reflection can copy the injection into new derived memories, and a larger window does not remove the cross-session store the attack lives in.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why intrinsic self-correction often fails
question: A first-pass agent is right 90% of the time. A self-review step fixes 30% of wrong answers but breaks 5% of right ones. What happens to accuracy?
options: Rises to 93%
Stays at 90%
Falls to 88.5%
Falls to 85.5%

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
question: With 256 containers and 100 s episodes you get 9216 rollouts per hour. Which change doubles throughput?
options: Doubling the group size G from 8 to 16
Halving the startup time from 20 s to 10 s
Halving the number of prompts per step
Doubling containers to 512 while episode time stays 100 s
explain: 512 x 3600 / 100 = 18432, exactly double. Halving startup only shortens episodes to 90 s (10240 per hour). Group size and prompts per step change how rollouts are used per step, not how many are produced per hour.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Direct and indirect injection, and how jailbreaks differ
question: Why do security teams treat indirect injection as more serious than a jailbreak, for an assistant with email access?
options: Because jailbreaks never work on modern models
Because the attacker can act through the victim's assistant, with the victim's data and tools, without ever logging in
Because indirect injection needs physical access
Because jailbreaks are illegal and injection is not
explain: A jailbreak mostly affects what the attacker themselves receives. Indirect injection turns someone else's assistant into the attacker's tool, inside the victim's privileges.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Approval gates and egress allowlists
question: What made Reprompt's "do every call twice" trick work?
options: Copilot cached the first answer
The leak safeguard checked only the first request, not later ones
The second request used a different user account
Browsers do not log repeated requests
explain: Varonis found the protection was applied only to the initial web request. Controls on outbound data must apply to every request, or the attacker simply asks again.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
question: Why can't a safetensors file run code when loaded?
options: Its format holds only a JSON header and raw numbers; the loader parses them and never calls functions named in the file
It is encrypted
Python refuses to open files over 1 MB
Hugging Face signs every safetensors file
explain: The format has no way to express "call this function". Pickle does (GLOBAL plus REDUCE). Note that safetensors does not prove where a model came from: that is what signing is for.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Defence in layers: privilege separation, provenance and egress
question: An agent must summarise web pages and also send emails for the user. Which design follows this lesson?
options: A quarantined model summarises pages with no tools; the email tool only accepts recipients that came from the user, and sends after approval
One model reads pages and sends emails, with a system prompt forbidding misuse
A keyword filter on page text before one model handles everything
Give the agent its own email account so the user's is safe
explain: Separating exposure from privilege, plus a provenance rule and an approval gate at the side effect, keeps a hijacked summariser from sending anything. Prompts and filters are useful layers, not the design.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
question: Why does MatterGen diffuse fractional coordinates with a wrapped Normal instead of an ordinary Gaussian?
options: Because wrapped Normals are cheaper to sample
Because fractional coordinates are periodic: x = 0.98 and x = 0.02 are close, and the noise must reach the uniform distribution on the cell
Because the lattice is always cubic during generation
Because atom types are discrete
explain: An ordinary Gaussian ignores that the cell wraps around: it pushes atoms outside [0, 1) and treats 0.98 and 0.02 as far apart. Wrapping folds probability mass back in, matches the minimum-image geometry from lesson 1, and gives a clean 'anywhere in the cell' noise limit.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
question: A watermarked model answers "What is 17 x 3?" with "51". Why will SynthID's mean g-value for this answer be close to 0.5?
options: The tournament only runs on outputs longer than 200 tokens
The model is almost certain of each token, so all candidates in the tournament are the same token and every match is decided by a coin flip
Numbers are excluded from the vocabulary hash
g-values are reset at the start of each response
explain: When p is concentrated on one token, all 2^m candidates are that token, so the output is fixed regardless of the g-values. The output's g-values are then just the token's pseudorandom values, averaging 0.5. Factual, low-entropy answers carry little watermark.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
question: In the tiny trace, what would change if line 8, free(b), were deleted?
options: Peak becomes 208 bytes
Nothing, because b was already counted
Live bytes at exit become 128 and b joins the leak report; the peak stays 144
Live bytes at exit become 64 and the peak drops
explain: free(b) happens after the peak, so the maximum of L(t) is still 144. Without it, 64 + 48 + 16 = 128 bytes are live at exit, and b is reported as leaked.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
question: A pipeline flags a daily row count as anomalous when |z| > 3, computed over the last 7 days including today. Today the count dropped to zero. Why might it never fire?
options: Because z-scores require normally distributed data and row counts are integers
Because with n = 7 the largest possible |z| is 6/sqrt(7), about 2.27, so |z| > 3 is impossible
Because the MAD of 7 values is always zero
Because a drop to zero is a negative deviation and z only detects increases
explain: The maximum |z| in a sample of n points is (n-1)/sqrt(n). For n = 7 that is about 2.27, so the rule can never trigger. Use a robust score computed on history that excludes today, or a longer window.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
question: A partner sends you their access token as `GET /report?access_token=...`. Which risk does RFC 6750 warn about?
options: The token is too short
URLs are stored in browser history and server logs and leak in Referer headers, so the token spreads to places that are not protected
Query strings are not encrypted by TLS
GET requests cannot carry tokens
explain: TLS does encrypt the query string on the wire. The problem is everywhere the URL is kept afterwards: logs, proxies, history, analytics, Referer headers. The header or body is the right place.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
question: Why does the client send the challenge (a hash) in the first redirect and the verifier only at the token endpoint?
options: The front-channel redirect can be observed or intercepted, so it carries only a value that cannot be reversed; the secret goes only on the direct TLS call
Hashes are shorter, so URLs stay under length limits
The token endpoint cannot compute SHA-256
To make the flow faster
explain: Anything in the browser redirect may leak (malicious apps, logs, history). SHA-256 cannot be inverted, so seeing the challenge does not reveal the verifier. Only the party that created the verifier can complete the exchange.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OpenID Connect: logging users in with an ID token
question: Why does the client compare the ID token's nonce with the value it stored?
options: To bind the ID token to the login this browser started, so a captured or injected ID token from another session is rejected
To decrypt the ID token
To measure network latency
To choose the signing algorithm
explain: The nonce travels in the authorization request and comes back inside the signed ID token. A token minted for a different request carries a different nonce, which is how OIDC prevents replay and injection.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and the forged Microsoft tokens (2023)
question: How did the first victim detect the intrusion?
options: Microsoft's antivirus flagged the actor
A user reported a phishing email
A custom alert on the MailItemsAccessed audit log showed mailbox access by an application that did not normally access mail
The forged tokens failed signature checks and caused errors
explain: The tokens worked perfectly, so there were no errors. The State Department's alert on an unusual AppId in MailItemsAccessed events was the signal, which CISA then described for other agencies in AA23-193A.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
question: A CISO wants to show the board that the company improved its threat modelling over a year, with a number. Which framework is built for that?
options: NIST SSDF, because it lists practices with task IDs
Microsoft SDL, because it has seven components
OWASP SAMM, because it scores each practice on maturity levels and supports a target per practice
None: security cannot be measured
explain: SAMM is a maturity model: it scores practices such as Threat Assessment from 0 to 3, so you can report current, target and progress. SSDF lists what to do, and SDL describes Microsoft's process; neither scores maturity.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Reviewing a real-looking diff: three bugs and their fixes
question: Why did neither scanner flag finding 3, the stored XSS?
options: XSS cannot be detected by any tool
The note endpoint has an ownership check, which scanners treat as a sanitiser
f-strings are invisible to static analysis
The source is a database row written earlier by another party, and default rules do not treat database reads as untrusted input
explain: Taint rules start from configured sources, usually request data. Stored XSS takes a detour through the database, which breaks the chain unless a rule marks those reads as sources. Reviewers must ask who wrote the data.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI
question: Why can IAST miss a vulnerability that SAST finds?
options: IAST only reports on code paths that tests or users actually executed during the run
IAST cannot run in CI
IAST only works on compiled languages
IAST ignores SQL
explain: IAST observes real execution, which makes its findings precise, but untested code is never observed. SAST reasons about all paths, including ones nobody executed, at the price of false positives.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Vulnerability management end to end: inventory, scans, deduplication
question: A scanner reports CVE-2021-44228 on a service whose only Log4j component is log4j-api 2.14.1. What should the pipeline do?
options: Open a critical ticket immediately
Mark it not applicable: Apache states only log4j-core is affected, and record the reason so the next scan does not reopen it
Delete the scanner
Upgrade Java
explain: Applicability checks cut noise. Recording the decision with its reason (Apache's advisory) keeps it from bouncing back on every scan; this is also what a VEX statement from the supply chain course expresses.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Programme decisions: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design
question: Why did Android's memory safety share fall sharply without rewriting most existing C and C++ code?
options: Rust compiles C code safely
Vulnerabilities concentrate in new code and decay with age, so writing new code in memory-safe languages cut the inflow while old code matured
Google stopped counting memory bugs
Old C++ code was deleted
explain: Google's post explains the drop by exponential decay of vulnerabilities with code age: stop adding new memory-unsafe code and the total falls even as the old code remains.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
question: Which statement about the redo pass is true?
options: It may read pages whose changes turn out to be on disk already
It writes a log record for every update it reapplies
It only reapplies changes of committed transactions
It starts at the BEGIN-CHECKPOINT record
explain: The DPT over-approximates, so some fetched pages (P1 and P2 here) need nothing. Redo logs nothing, repeats loser changes too, and starts at the smallest recLSN, which can be before the checkpoint.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
question: Under correct roles, why does the duplicate question D1 still score 0.83 with Q1?
options: Because query mode is applied to D1 by mistake
Because cosine similarity of any two questions is at least 0.8
Because the role changes how form and answer content are weighted but the shared France topic still aligns the vectors
Because D1 is longer than Q1
explain: Role encoding reweights features; it does not remove topic. D1 really is about the capital of France, so it stays a strong candidate. What changes is that the answer passage now scores higher, by a margin of 0.14 in this toy.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
question: On OpenAI you set `max_tokens` to a very large value "just in case", though responses average 200 tokens. What is the rate-limit effect?
options: None, only generated tokens are counted
Each request is counted against the token limit using the larger of max_tokens and the estimated size, so you hit TPM much sooner than your real usage implies
The request is rejected with 400 because max_tokens exceeds the response
Output becomes slower but the limit is unaffected
explain: OpenAI's rate-limit guide says the limit is based on the larger of max_tokens and the token count estimated from the request, and advises setting max_tokens close to the expected size. Anthropic documents the opposite for OTPM: max_tokens is not counted, only generated tokens.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
question: A service has 20,000 open WebSocket connections that are idle 99% of the time, plus a CPU-heavy image resize per request. Which statement is right?
options: Async makes the image resize itself run faster because tasks switch without the kernel
Async lets idle connections cost a small state object each, but the resize still needs real CPU time and must not hog a runtime thread
Async only helps if every connection is busy all the time
Thread per connection and async use the same memory, since both store a stack per connection
explain: The win is for *waiting*. Idle connections become small suspended futures instead of 20,000 thread stacks. CPU work takes the same CPU time either way, and lesson 5 shows why long CPU work on a runtime thread hurts every other task.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
question: A Tokio service on 8 cores calls a synchronous database driver directly in each request handler. Load tests with 4 concurrent requests look fine; production with 200 concurrent requests shows multi-second latency spikes even for /health. What is the best fix?
options: Raise event_interval so the I/O driver runs more often
Run the driver calls in spawn_blocking (or use an async driver) so worker threads keep polling other tasks
Switch to the current-thread runtime to avoid stealing overhead
Call tokio::task::yield_now() before each query
explain: Each blocking query pins a worker. With 8 workers, 8 slow queries freeze every other task, including /health. Moving blocking calls to the blocking pool (or an async client) frees the workers. yield_now before the query does not help because the blocking happens after it.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses
question: You need a shared counter of processed requests, incremented by 32 worker threads. Which choice fits best?
options: A CAS loop, because CAS is the most general primitive
A mutex around a plain integer, because atomics are undefined behavior with more than two threads
fetch_add(1, Relaxed), because it never retries and expresses exactly the update
A volatile integer with ++
explain: fetch_add does the whole read-modify-write in one operation that cannot fail, so there are no wasted attempts under contention. A CAS loop is correct but retries under contention. A mutex works but costs more. volatile ++ is a data race.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: AST and SpecAugment: patches, attention and masked bands
question: Using AST's formula, how many patches does a 5 s clip produce?
explain: $100t - 16 = 484$, divided by 10 and rounded up gives 49 patch columns; times 12 rows gives 588. The 10 s case gives 1188.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
question: The salt is stored in the same database row as the hash. An attacker steals the whole table. Does that defeat the salt?
options: Yes: knowing the salt lets the attacker reverse the hash
Yes: the attacker can now use a precomputed rainbow table
No: the salt still forces separate work per user and makes precomputed tables useless
No, but only because salts are encrypted
explain: A salt was never meant to be secret. Its value is that it is unique: precomputed tables did not include it, and every user must be attacked separately. Secrecy is the job of a pepper (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
question: Which change fixes session fixation?
options: Making session IDs longer
Setting the HttpOnly flag on the cookie
Issuing a new session ID when the user logs in
Adding an idle timeout of 15 minutes
explain: Fixation works because the ID chosen before login stays valid after it. Regenerating the ID at login means the attacker's known ID never becomes authenticated. Longer IDs, HttpOnly and timeouts help against other attacks but not this one.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
question: Why did MFA not stop the Twitter 2020 attackers?
options: Twitter did not use MFA at the time
The attackers cracked Twitter's password hashes offline
The attackers relayed the employee's credentials to the real site in real time, and the employee approved the resulting MFA prompt
The attackers guessed the 6-digit codes
explain: The NYDFS report describes a live relay: credentials typed into a look-alike VPN page were entered into the real site at once, and the real MFA prompt was approved by the employee. A typed or approved factor is not bound to the site.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
question: A lead agent sends three subagents the task "research the chip shortage". The results overlap heavily and one sub-question is never covered. What is the best fix?
options: Spawn ten subagents so coverage is more likely
Run the three subagents sequentially so they can read each other's notes
Raise the subagents' temperature to diversify their searches
Give each subagent an objective, output format, source guidance and explicit boundaries that exclude the others' topics
explain: This is the failure Anthropic described: vague task descriptions lead to duplicated work and gaps. Detailed, bounded task descriptions fix the division of labor. Temperature sets how random the output is: the model's next-token scores are divided by it before becoming probabilities, so a higher value flattens them. More agents or more randomness would increase cost without guaranteeing coverage, and running sequentially gives up the speedup.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
question: Why does PaperBench grade results produced by re-running `reproduce.sh` in a fresh environment rather than the files the agent left behind?
options: Fresh environments are faster to grade
It stops an agent from scoring result-match leaves with numbers it wrote by hand during its run
The LLM judge cannot read files from the agent's environment
It ensures the agent used the blacklisted official code
explain: Separating reproduction from the agent's run means only results the code actually produces are graded, which closes a direct reward-hacking route: writing the expected numbers into a results file. Blacklisted code is forbidden, not required.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
question: Why would a LoRA-adapted model be cheaper to serve on demand than a fully fine-tuned one, in the AWS Nova customization flow?
options: LoRA models have fewer layers
LoRA removes the need for a tokenizer
Full fine-tunes cannot be imported into Bedrock
Only small adapter weights differ from the shared base, so the AWS post says PEFT models run on demand while full fine-tunes use Provisioned Throughput
explain: The adapters are small and the base is shared, so per-token on-demand serving works. A full fine-tune changes every weight, which needs its own dedicated copy. The AWS post says full fine-tunes can also be imported, but they run with Provisioned Throughput.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Symbols, stripping and debug info: what survives
question: A stripped, dynamically linked ELF binary calls `connect` and `SSL_write`. Will those names appear in `nm -D` output?
options: No, strip removes all names
Yes, imported functions stay in .dynsym because the dynamic loader must resolve them at run time
Only if the binary was built with -g
Only on Mach-O
explain: The dynamic symbol table is part of what the program needs to run, so strip cannot delete it. Imports are a reliable map of behaviour even in stripped binaries.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Compiler idioms: multiply to divide, tables and branchless code
question: A switch with six cases appears in the binary as a bounds check and a single `ldr w0, [x1, w0, uxtw #2]`. What do you conclude about the source?
options: The switch called six different functions
Each case returned a constant, so the compiler built a lookup table
The code is obfuscated
The switch had no default
explain: A data load (not an indirect branch) means the table holds values, not code addresses. A jump table ends in br/blr on ARM64 or jmp [table] on x86-64.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Go binaries: the runtime, stack checks and pclntab
question: Why can't `-ldflags="-s -w"` remove function names from a Go binary?
options: It is a linker bug
Go encrypts names
The runtime itself reads pclntab while running, for panic stack traces and FuncForPC, so the names in it must stay
Because Go binaries are dynamically linked
explain: -s removes the ELF symbol table and debug info, which only tools use. pclntab is data the program itself reads while running.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Inside extracted firmware: boot chain, filesystem and findings
question: A Linux router shows a process named `[kworker/0:1]` whose /proc entry points to a deleted file. What does that suggest?
options: A normal kernel worker thread
A crashed process
A filesystem error only
A user-space program disguised as a kernel thread, running from a file that was deleted after launch: a strong sign of compromise
explain: A /proc exe link means the process was started from a program file, so it is user-space code whatever its name says; the deleted file means someone removed the evidence. KV-botnet used exactly this masquerade and deletion.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
question: A ternary weight row has 1000 entries, 350 of them zero. Roughly what arithmetic does one output need?
options: 1000 multiplies and 999 adds
350 integer adds and 650 multiplies
650 multiplies, since zeros are skipped
650 integer adds or subtracts, then 1 multiply by the combined scale
explain: Each +1 adds the activation, each -1 subtracts it, each 0 is skipped: about 650 integer add or subtract steps. The scales gamma and s are shared, so they are applied once to the final sum.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
question: Your hot loop has `if (x[i] > threshold)` where x is random noise and the condition is true 50 percent of the time. A teammate suggests buying a CPU with a better branch predictor. Expected effect on this branch?
options: Big win, newer predictors use longer history
Small win, perceptrons can learn noise
About nothing, it will still miss about 50 percent of the time
It gets worse, longer history adds noise
explain: With independent 50/50 outcomes there is no pattern to learn. Agner's measurements for a random 50/50 branch give a 0.500 misprediction rate. Removing the branch (lesson 4) is the fix, not a better predictor.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
question: Adding `__builtin_expect(x > 0, 1)` to a branch that is truly 50/50 random will:
options: Make the hardware predictor guess taken, fixing the misses
Turn the branch into a cmov
Cause a compile error for non-constant expressions
Change code layout at most; the branch still misses about half the time
explain: The hint informs the compiler's code layout and optimization decisions. The hardware's dynamic predictor still sees a random sequence and misses about 50 percent. To fix a random branch, remove it with a select, mask or table.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
question: A team moves a write-heavy service to an LSM engine. After a week, p99 read latency (the 99th percentile: 99% of reads are faster than it) climbs steadily while the write rate is constant, and disk utilization is at 100%. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bloom filters have too many bits per key
Compaction is not keeping up, so L0 files and sorted runs accumulate and each read checks more of them
The memtable is too small to hold recent writes
The WAL is being fsynced too rarely
explain: Rising read latency at a constant write rate with a saturated disk is the signature of compaction debt: more L0 files and runs per lookup, and compaction I/O competing with reads. More Bloom bits would help reads, not hurt them; WAL fsync policy affects durability and write latency.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
question: Why do O'Neil et al. recommend K = 2 rather than K = 3 for general use?
options: K = 3 never beats K = 2 on any workload
K = 3 cannot be implemented with a priority queue
K = 3 turns into plain LRU when the pool is large
K = 3 needs more references before it adapts when access frequencies change
explain: The paper reports that LRU-3 comes closer to the optimal policy on stable patterns, but it needs more references to adapt to changing frequencies. K = 2 is the practical balance.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: MTD, RTO and RPO: the arithmetic and the dependency trap
question: The ordering process has an MTD of 24 h and needs 4 h of data reprocessing after any restore. Its database restores in 10 h, but identity takes 16 h and must be up first. What should happen?
options: Nothing: the database's 10 h is well under 24 h
Set ordering's RTO to 24 h, since that is the MTD
Record a gap: the critical path is at least 26 h against a 20 h RTO budget, so identity recovery must get faster
Drop the reprocessing step from the plan
explain: The RTO budget is 24 - 4 = 20 h. With identity first, ordering cannot be back before 16 + 10 = 26 h, so the plan misses. SP 800-34 says to track this with a plan of action and milestones, and the fix belongs to identity, a shared dependency.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
question: Atlassian's script passed peer review and a staging test. Which control would most directly have stopped the deletion of whole sites?
options: A longer peer review
Running the script more slowly
An API that checks the type of each ID and refuses site IDs when the operation is an app deletion
Encrypting the site IDs
explain: The root problem was an API that accepted both site and app IDs and assumed the input was right. Reviewers looked at the call, not the data; staging lacked the production IDs. A typed check at the point of deletion catches the mix-up whatever the process upstream.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
question: Microsoft's recovery tool offered a safe mode option that could avoid typing BitLocker recovery keys. What did it need instead?
options: An account with local administrator rights on each device
Internet access on each device
A CrowdStrike license key
Nothing: it bypassed BitLocker
explain: Safe mode works on TPM-only protected devices because the TPM still unlocks the disk, but running the fix needs local admin rights. TPM+PIN devices still need the PIN or the recovery key. Nothing bypasses BitLocker; that is its purpose.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
question: Why can a byte-level model never hit an out-of-vocabulary input?
options: Its vocabulary is the 256 possible byte values, and any UTF-8 text is a sequence of bytes
It learns new tokens during inference
It maps rare characters to an UNK id
UTF-8 has only 256 characters
explain: Every string, in any script, is a sequence of bytes 0 to 255, so the input vocabulary is complete by construction. UTF-8 covers all of Unicode by using 1 to 4 bytes per character, not by having 256 characters.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
question: You serve a model under a fixed inference FLOP budget per byte. Why can BLT use a bigger model than a BPE model in the same budget?
options: Byte embeddings are smaller than token embeddings
The entropy model replaces some latent layers
Bigger average patches mean fewer latent steps per byte, so each step can afford more parameters
BLT skips the softmax at inference
explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Raising P from about 3.7 (Llama 2 tokens) to 8 lowers the m_g/P term, so m_g can grow while cost per byte stays fixed: 760M versus 470M in the paper's small class. BPE can only lengthen tokens by growing the vocabulary.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
question: Why is `RefCell<T>` Send (when T is Send) but not Sync?
options: RefCell allocates on the heap, which threads cannot share
Its borrow flag is updated without atomics: moving it leaves one thread in charge, but sharing `&RefCell` lets two threads update the flag at once
Sync requires a type to have no methods that take `&mut self`
RefCell panics on conflicting borrows, and panics cannot cross threads
explain: Moving a RefCell to another thread leaves exactly one thread able to touch it, so Send is fine. Sync means `&RefCell<T>` could be used from two threads at once, and its run-time borrow bookkeeping is ordinary non-atomic memory: that would be a data race.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
question: A C library returns `char *` from `lib_get_name()` and documents that callers must release it with `lib_free_name()`. How should the Rust wrapper free it?
options: Call `lib_free_name` (for example from a `Drop` impl) after copying the bytes out
Wrap it with `CString::from_raw` and let Rust drop it
Call `libc::free`, since all C strings come from malloc
Leave it: Rust frees foreign memory automatically at scope end
explain: `CString::from_raw` is only for pointers produced by `CString::into_raw`; on foreign memory it risks allocator corruption. The library may not use malloc at all, so its own release function is the only correct one. Rust never frees memory it does not own.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
question: An L1 has a 4-cycle hit time and a 10% miss rate, and every miss costs 100 more cycles. What is the AMAT?
options: 4.4 cycles
10.4 cycles
14 cycles
40 cycles
explain: AMAT = 4 + 0.10 x 100 = 14 cycles. 4.4 forgets that the penalty is 100 cycles, not 4; 40 multiplies instead of adding. Note how a 10% miss rate more than triples the hit time.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
question: What does a transcoder learn to approximate?
options: The residual stream at the same layer, from itself
The output of an MLP layer, computed from that MLP's input
The attention pattern of every head in the layer
The final logits, computed from the embeddings
explain: A transcoder maps MLP input to MLP output through a wide sparse layer, so it can stand in for the MLP. An SAE reconstructs the same activation it reads, which describes but does not replace the computation.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
question: You raise the node threshold from 0.8 to 0.95 on a real prompt. What should you expect?
options: Fewer nodes and higher completeness
The same nodes, because embeddings dominate
More nodes and lower completeness
More nodes and higher completeness
explain: A higher threshold keeps more of the influence. On one acronym prompt the paper reports 55 nodes and completeness 0.70 at 0.8, versus 236 nodes and 0.87 at 0.95: easier to explain more, harder to read.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
question: To explain why a model hallucinated about an unknown name, which approach does the biology paper suggest is needed beyond a single attribution graph?
options: Raise the pruning threshold until the cause appears
Remove all error nodes
Compare contrastive prompts (known vs unknown entity) to find features that should have been active but were suppressed
Use only direct edges to the logit
explain: Graphs list active features. A hallucination can come from a "can't answer" feature being wrongly inhibited, so you need a counterfactual (Michael Jordan vs Michael Batkin) to find the inactive feature and its inhibitors.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
question: You clip at tau = 0.2 with theta_k = 1/k. A document at rank 10 has relevance 0.6. What does its clipped estimate converge to?
explain: Expected value is gamma x theta / tau = 0.6 x 0.1 / 0.2 = 0.3. With infinite data the bias stays: the document looks half as relevant as it is.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck
question: A site stores comments exactly as typed and encodes them when rendering the blog page. A new admin dashboard shows the latest comments using a different template that does not encode. What is the risk?
options: Stored XSS that runs in administrators' browsers, with administrator privileges
None, because the comments were safe on the blog page
Only the attacker sees the payload, so it is self-XSS
The database will reject the comment the second time it is read
explain: Safety is a property of each output path, not of the stored data. The dashboard is a new sink, and its viewers have the most powerful sessions in the system, which makes this one of the worst places for stored XSS.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: When users need HTML: sanitising with DOMPurify
question: Why does DOMPurify parse the HTML with the browser's own parser instead of matching patterns in the string?
options: So that it inspects the same tree the browser will actually build, rather than guessing how the browser will read the string
Parsing is faster than regular expressions
Because regular expressions are not available in JavaScript
To convert the HTML to plain text
explain: Pattern filters fail when the browser parses the string differently from the filter's assumptions, as MySpace's did. Checking the real parsed tree removes that guesswork, which is why allowlist sanitisers built on the DOM are the recommended approach.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Open redirects, and clickjacking revisited
question: A developer validates `next` with `next.startsWith("/")`. Which input still sends users off-site?
options: //evil.example/login
/orders
/account/settings
/?ref=email
explain: Two leading slashes form a protocol-relative URL: the browser keeps the current scheme and treats evil.example as the host. Parsing with new URL() and comparing the origin catches it, because the parser and the browser agree.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
question: Why should a dashboard that displays CSP reports never insert report fields as HTML?
options: Anyone can POST fake reports, so fields like sample are attacker-controlled data, and rendering them raw would put stored XSS in the security team's own tool
Reports are too large for HTML
Browsers encrypt report fields
CSP reports are binary, not text
explain: The report endpoint is public by design. Treat every field as untrusted input and render it as text, or the monitoring tool becomes the next stored XSS victim, with the security team's sessions at stake.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
question: A photo search built on CLIP returns, for the query 'three dogs on a beach', many images with one or two dogs. Which explanation is best supported by the sources?
options: The index is approximate, so it drops the best matches
The logit scale was not applied at query time
CLIP embeddings encode counts poorly; the paper reports it struggles with counting objects
The text encoder truncates queries longer than 3 words
explain: The CLIP paper lists counting among its systematic weaknesses (CLEVRCounts). The logit scale does not affect the ranking, the text encoder accepts up to 76 tokens, and an approximate index would not systematically return the wrong count.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Capital One 2019 replayed through the logs
question: Which single field in the March 2019 CloudTrail events most clearly separated the attacker's activity from the firewall's normal activity?
options: eventName, because ListBuckets is always malicious
userIdentity.type, because AssumedRole means an attacker
awsRegion, because attackers always use other Regions
sourceIPAddress: a role meant for one instance being used from Tor and VPN addresses
explain: The WAF role legitimately produced AssumedRole events every day, and ListBuckets can be routine. What was abnormal was where the session was used from: instance credentials calling the API from Tor exits and a VPN provider. GuardDuty's InstanceCredentialExfiltration finding encodes exactly that.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: SCARLETEEL 2023: from a Kubernetes pod to the AWS account
question: In SCARLETEEL, which control would have stopped the attacker from turning one exploited pod into AWS API access?
options: Encrypting the S3 buckets with KMS
Requiring IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1 and giving pods their own narrowly scoped roles instead of the node's
Enabling CloudTrail data events
Rotating the Terraform state key every 90 days
explain: The step from pod to cloud was the node role's credentials from IMDSv1. IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 blocked that from inside containers in SCARLETEEL 2.0, and per-pod roles remove the node role from the pod's reach. Encryption and data events do not stop the theft; rotation would not prevent first use.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Uber 2022: from one contractor's login to the cloud consoles
question: A PAM vault administrator account was compromised for three hours. Logs show the attacker viewed 4 of the vault's 300 secrets. What should be rotated?
options: Only the 4 secrets viewed
None, if the vault's audit log is complete
All 300 secrets, prioritising the 4 viewed and any cloud administrator credentials
Only the vault administrator's own password
explain: An administrator could export or reveal secrets in ways the audit trail may not fully capture, and could create persistence. Treat everything reachable as exposed, rotate the confirmed four and the most powerful first, then the rest.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Landing zones: an account layout that contains failure
question: Where should the organization's authoritative CloudTrail logs be stored?
options: In each workload account, so its admins can manage them
In a Log Archive account in the Security OU, which workload administrators cannot change
In the management account, which SCPs cannot restrict
In the Sandbox account, where storage is cheapest
explain: AWS's whitepaper describes the Log Archive account as the consolidation point for every account's logs. Logs in the account they describe can be deleted by whoever compromises that account; the management account should hold no workloads or data.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: IAM privilege escalation: the classes behind Rhino's 21 methods
question: A role has `iam:PassRole` on `*`, `lambda:CreateFunction` and `lambda:CreateEventSourceMapping`, but not `lambda:InvokeFunction`. Is there an escalation path?
options: No, because without InvokeFunction the function can never run
Only if the role also has iam:AttachRolePolicy
No, because Lambda refuses roles with administrator permissions
Yes: pass a powerful role to a new function and let an event source such as a DynamoDB stream trigger it
explain: This is Rhino's method 16: an event source mapping invokes the function without the attacker calling InvokeFunction. The fix is scoping PassRole by resource and iam:PassedToService, not removing one invoke permission.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets
question: A team stores the database password as a Lambda environment variable, encrypted with the default AWS managed key. Who can read it?
options: Only the function itself
Nobody, because environment variables are encrypted
Only the AWS account root user
Any principal allowed to read the function's configuration, since GetFunctionConfiguration returns the variables
explain: Encryption at rest does not hide values from callers allowed to read the configuration. AWS recommends Secrets Manager for credentials; a customer managed key at least restricts viewing to users who can use that key.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: CSPM, CIEM and CNAPP, and a full architecture review
question: Which of these is a CIEM capability rather than CSPM?
options: Checking that storage encryption is enabled
Scanning a container image for vulnerable packages
Checking that logging is turned on in every Region
Mapping which identities can reach which resources, including through chains of roles
explain: CIEM is about entitlements: who can access what. Encryption and logging checks are posture (CSPM); image scanning is workload protection (CWPP).

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
question: Which of these can appear in the `Principal` element of a bucket policy?
options: An IAM group
An IAM role ARN
An OU name
A security group
explain: Principals are authenticated identities such as users, roles, accounts and services. Groups only collect permissions for users and cannot be principals.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Instance roles at scale: IMDSv2 everywhere and a data perimeter
question: The RequireSameVPC policy is attached as an SCP. An attacker steals an instance role's credentials through an SSRF bug and uses them from a home internet connection. What happens to their S3 calls?
options: They are denied only if MFA is required
They are denied, because the request's source VPC does not match the VPC the credentials were delivered to
They succeed until the credentials expire
They succeed, because the role allows S3
explain: Requests from outside carry no matching aws:SourceVpc, so the explicit Deny in the SCP applies and overrides the role's Allow. The credentials are valid but useless outside their network.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Network controls: VPCs, security groups and private endpoints
question: A security group on a database allows inbound TCP 5432 from the web tier's security group only. There are no other rules. A request arrives from the internet on port 5432. What happens?
options: It is blocked, because only explicitly allowed traffic gets in and security groups cannot even express a deny
It is allowed if the database password is correct
It is blocked only if a network ACL also denies it
It is allowed, because security groups allow by default
explain: Security groups contain only allow rules; anything not matched is dropped before it reaches the database.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
question: A role's temporary credentials leaked through an application log. Which action stops sessions already issued?
options: Revoking active sessions, which attaches AWSRevokeOlderSessions to deny sessions issued before now
Deactivating the root user's access keys
Waiting for MFA to expire
Deleting the role's trust policy
explain: Temporary credentials cannot be deactivated individually like access keys. Revoking sessions adds a policy denying all sessions issued before that time; new, legitimate sessions continue to work.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
question: A clustering gives point q a silhouette of -0.35. What does that say?
options: q is an outlier that belongs to no cluster
The clustering has too few clusters, since silhouettes cannot be negative otherwise
q is exactly on the boundary between two clusters
q is on average closer to the points of another cluster than to the points of its own
explain: Negative means b(i) is less than a(i): the mean distance to the nearest other cluster is smaller than the mean distance to its own cluster members. A value near 0, not negative, means a boundary point. The silhouette has no notion of noise, and negative values can appear at any k.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Clustering embeddings of logs and incidents
question: Raw TF-IDF vectors of log lines are clustered with k-means and one cluster contains only the single longest message, while everything else is in one huge cluster. What is the first thing to fix?
options: Increase k until the huge cluster breaks apart
Switch from k-means to DBSCAN with the default eps
L2 normalise the vectors so that message length stops dominating the geometry
Lower n_init to 1 so the run is faster and more stable
explain: That failure is the e1 case: an unnormalised vector with a large norm sits far from the origin and from everything else, so it earns its own centroid. Normalisation projects everything onto the unit sphere and leaves only direction. Raising k or switching algorithm without fixing the representation keeps the same bad geometry, and DBSCAN's default eps of 0.5 is meaningless for an unknown scale.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Parquet on disk: row groups, column chunks, pages and a footer
question: Why does Parquet put the file metadata at the end of the file instead of the start?
options: Readers must scan the data before they can parse the schema
So the writer can stream row groups out in a single pass and record their offsets and stats afterwards
Because Thrift requires trailing headers
To make appends to an existing file cheap
explain: The spec says metadata is written after the data to allow single-pass writing: chunk offsets and statistics are only known once the chunks are written. Readers simply read the last 8 bytes first.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
question: A table is written as Parquet with 1 GB row groups and no page index, written in random order. Queries filter on customer_id = X and read 3 of 50 columns. Which change most reduces bytes read?
options: Enable AVX-512 in the query engine
Increase the engine's vector size to 1M
Convert the files to Arrow IPC for storage
Sort or cluster by customer_id when writing (and write a page index) so min/max stats can skip most groups and pages
explain: Column projection already limits reads to 3 columns. The remaining waste is reading groups that cannot contain X; clustering makes min/max ranges narrow so pruning works. SIMD and vector size affect CPU, not bytes read.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
question: A hash function multiplies `int h` by a large constant and relies on it wrapping. At -O2 a later check on h behaves strangely. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Compile that file at -O0
Declare h volatile
Switch to -O3
Make h unsigned: unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap
explain: Signed overflow is UB at every level, so -O0 only hides it and a later compiler may break it again. volatile changes memory access, not arithmetic rules. Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2 to the bit width, which is exactly what a hash wants.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
question: You collect a PGO profile by running only the test suite, which mostly exercises error paths. What is likely to happen on production traffic?
options: Production gets the full PGO speedup anyway
The compiler refuses the profile
The binary crashes on untested paths
The hot production paths may be treated as cold and optimized for size or laid out poorly
explain: PGO trusts the counts. Paths the profile never saw look cold, so they may be laid out away from hot code and inlined less. Profile with inputs that represent the real workload.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Grounding: Set-of-Mark labels, DOM and accessibility trees
question: Your agent uses SoM marks generated from the accessibility tree. In a canvas-based drawing app, the tree contains only the window frame. What happens?
options: The model falls back to clicking marks on the frame, which is fine
There are no marks for the canvas content, so the agent needs raw pixel coordinates (and zoom) there
SoM segments the canvas automatically from the tree's bounding boxes
The accessibility API generates synthetic nodes for drawn shapes
explain: SoM over GUIs is only as good as the element source. If the tree exposes no nodes for drawn content, there is nothing to mark. Image segmentation (as in the original SoM paper) or direct pixel grounding are the remaining options.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
question: In a loom test, thread A does `x.load(Acquire)` and thread B does `x.load(Acquire)` on the same atomic, with nothing else in between. How many orders of these two loads must loom explore?
options: One: two loads of the same location do not conflict, so both orders behave the same
Two: A then B, and B then A
Zero: loads are never scheduling points
It depends on LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS
explain: Reordering two reads of the same location cannot change what either one returns, so the second order is equivalent and loom skips it. A load and a store, or two stores, do conflict and both orders are explored.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
question: A TSan report shows the current stack but says *failed to restore the stack* for the previous access. What do you change?
options: Set halt_on_error=1
Add -O3 to the build
Increase history_size in TSAN_OPTIONS
Set report_atomic_races=0
explain: The previous access's stack comes from a per-thread history buffer. The Clang docs say to increase `history_size` (0 to 7) when you see this message.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
question: A system acknowledges a write, then a different client starts a read 5 seconds later and gets the old value. Which statement is correct?
options: This is always a bug in any replicated database
Whether it is allowed depends on the consistency model the system promises
It is allowed only if the two clients talk to the same replica
It cannot happen if the write was durably persisted
explain: A consistency model defines the allowed histories. Under eventual consistency (lesson 5), which only promises that replicas agree once writes stop, this stale read is legal. Under linearizability it is forbidden, because the read started after the write completed. Durability is a separate property: DynamoDB, for example, persists a write before acknowledging it, yet its default reads may still miss it.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Eventual consistency, session guarantees and real systems
question: A shopping cart service lets users add items while their phone is offline and syncs later. Which model fits, and what must you design for?
options: Strong eventual consistency; design how concurrent updates merge
Linearizability; design for leader failover
Sequential consistency; design a global order of carts
Read your writes only; no merging is needed
explain: Offline writes rule out any model that needs a quorum, so linearizable and sequential are out. With replicas accepting writes independently, concurrent edits will conflict, and convergence requires a deterministic merge (a CRDT or last-writer-wins, which can drop data).

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
question: A counter key receives 50,000 increments per second; a shard can absorb 8,000 writes per second. Which fix actually works?
options: Add more shards to the ring
Give the shard more virtual nodes
Split the counter into 10 sub-counters with suffixes and sum them on read
Put a client-side read cache in front of it
explain: A single key lives on one shard, so more shards or tokens cannot divide its traffic. A read cache does nothing for writes. Splitting into 10 sub-keys spreads about 5,000 writes per second to each (if they hash to different shards), and the price is that a read must fetch and add all 10.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Weighting soft scores with function_score and phased ranking
question: In our function_score query, what is the effect of `"boost_mode": "replace"`?
options: The final score is the combined function score; the wrapped query's score is ignored
The filters are replaced by the functions
Each function's weight replaces its own output
Missing fields are replaced by the origin
explain: boost_mode decides how the function result combines with the query score; replace uses only the function score. Here the wrapped query is filter-only and scores 0, so the default multiply would make every final score 0.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
question: In the example, what makes x5 the first UIP of the conflict?
options: It was the first literal assigned at level 3
It is the only level-3 node that every path from the decision x3 to the conflict passes through, closest to the conflict
It appears in the most clauses of the formula
It has the highest VSIDS activity
explain: A unique implication point at the conflict level is a node every path from that level's decision to the conflict goes through. The decision x3 is always one; the first UIP is the one nearest the conflict, here x5. Cutting there gives (not x4 or not x5), which is shorter and more general than the decision-only clause.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
question: Your scanner reports no vulnerabilities for an image built last month. What should you conclude?
options: The image has no bugs
No currently published advisory matches a package the scanner recognised; rescan regularly because new CVEs are published every day
The image will stay clean
Scanning is unnecessary for this image
explain: A scan is a snapshot against today's databases and only covers packages it can identify. New advisories appear constantly, so running images need continuous rescanning.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
question: Your cluster's kubelets run without seccompDefault. A pod spec sets no seccompProfile. Which seccomp profile does it get?
options: RuntimeDefault
Docker's default profile
Unconfined
Localhost
explain: The Kubernetes seccomp tutorial says pods use RuntimeDefault by default only when seccompDefault is enabled; otherwise the default is Unconfined. Set it in the pod or enable the kubelet option.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
question: A namespace has `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A user applies a Deployment whose pod template sets `privileged: true`. What happens?
options: The Deployment is accepted, but its pods are rejected when the ReplicaSet tries to create them
PSA mutates the template to remove privileged
The pods start but are killed after 60 seconds
The Deployment is rejected immediately
explain: The PSA docs state enforce applies only to the resulting pod objects, while audit and warn also apply to workload resources. PSA validates; it never mutates.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
question: Which control blocked CVE-2019-5736 even on unpatched runc, according to the advisory?
options: Network policies
The default AppArmor profile
A read-only root filesystem
User namespaces where the host's root is not mapped into the container
explain: The advisory says it is not blocked by the default AppArmor policy but is blocked by correct use of user namespaces: container root is then not host root, so it cannot write the host runc binary.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
question: The last instruction in a build deletes a 300 MB cache directory that an earlier instruction created. What happens to the size of the pushed image?
options: It shrinks by 300 MB, because the final filesystem no longer contains the directory
The build fails, because whiteouts may not refer to lower layers
The earlier layer is rewritten without the directory
